{{Short description|Extinct language of Texas and Mexico}} {{Infobox language | name = Coahuilteco | states = [[Mexico]], [[United States]] | region = [[Coahuila]], [[Texas]] | ethnicity = [[Quems]], [[Pajalat]], etc. | extinct = 18th century | familycolor = hokan | fam1 = [[Hokan languages|Hokan]] ? | fam2 = [[Coahuiltecan languages|Coahuiltecan]] ? | fam3 = [[Pakawan]] ? | iso3 = xcw | linglist = xcw | glotto = coah1252 | glottorefname = Coahuilteco | dia1 = Pajalat | map = Coahuilteco lang.png | mapcaption = Coauhuilteco language | notice = IPA | image = Cuaderno_lengua_indios_pajalates.pdf | imagecaption = Manuscript of the Pajalate (Coahuilteco) language | altname = Pajalate | family = [[Language isolate]] }} '''Coahuilteco''' was one of the Indigenous languages that was spoken in southern [[Texas]] (United States) and northeastern [[Coahuila]] (Mexico). It is now [[Extinct language|extinct]], and is typically considered to be a language isolate,{{Cite thesis|last=Acosta |first=Miguel R. |date=2022 |title=Coahuilteco Language Reclamation Program |url=https://repository.arizona.edu/handle/10150/667945 |language=en}}{{Citation |last=Troike |first=Rudolph C. |title=Sketch of Coahuilteco, a Language Isolate of Texas |date=1996 |work=Languages |volume=17 |pages=644–665 |url=https://theswissbay.ch/pdf/Books/Linguistics/Mega%20linguistics%20pack/North%20American/Other/Coahuilteco%2C%20Sketch%20of%20%28Troike%29.pdf |access-date=2025-06-12 |series=Handbook of North American Indians |place=Washington |publisher=Washington, D.C.: Smithsonian Institution}} but has also been proposed to be part of a [[Pakawan languages|Pakawan]] family. ==Classification== Coahuilteco was grouped in an eponymous [[Coahuiltecan languages|Coahuiltecan]] family by [[John Wesley Powell]] in 1891, later expanded by additional proposed members by e.g. [[Edward Sapir]]. [[Ives Goddard]] later treated all these connections with suspicion, leaving Coahuilteco as a [[language isolate]]. Manaster Ramer (1996) argues Powell's original more narrow Coahuiltecan grouping is sound, renaming it Pakawan in distinction from the later more expanded proposal.{{Cite journal|last=Ramer|first=Alexis Manaster|date=1996|title=Sapir's Classifications: Coahuiltecan|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/30028442|journal=Anthropological Linguistics|volume=38|issue=1|pages=1–38|jstor=30028442|issn=0003-5483}} This proposal has been challenged by Campbell,{{Cite journal|last=Campbell|first=Lyle|date=1996|title=Coahuiltecan: A Closer Look|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/30013048|journal=Anthropological Linguistics|volume=38|issue=4|pages=620–634|jstor=30013048|issn=0003-5483}} who considers its sound correspondences unsupported and considers that some of the observed similarities between words may be due to borrowing. It is now considered a language isolate.{{Citation |last=Zamponi |first=Raoul |title=5 Extinct lineages and unclassified languages of Mexico |date=2024-12-02 |work=The Languages and Linguistics of Mexico and Northern Central America |pages=99–158 |editor-last=Wichmann |editor-first=Søren |url=https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/9783110421705-005/html |access-date=2025-06-08 |publisher=De Gruyter |doi=10.1515/9783110421705-005 |isbn=978-3-11-042170-5|url-access=subscription }} ==Phonology== ===Consonants=== {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;" ! colspan="2" rowspan="2" | ! rowspan="2" | [[Bilabial consonant|Bilabial]] ! rowspan="2" | [[Interdental consonant|Inter-

[[Open vowel|Open]] | | {{IPAlink|a|a / aː}} | |} Coahuilteco has both short and long vowels.Troike, 1996 == Syntax == Based primarily on study of one 88-page document, Fray Bartolomé García's 1760 ''Manual para administrar los santos sacramentos de penitencia, eucharistia, extrema-uncion, y matrimonio: dar gracias despues de comulgar, y ayudar a bien morir,'' Troike describes two of Coahuilteco's less common syntactic traits: subject-object concord and center-embedding relative clauses.{{Cite journal|last=Troike|first=Rudolph C.|date=1981|title=Subject-Object Concord in Coahuilteco|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/414344|journal=Language|volume=57|issue=3|pages=658–673|doi=10.2307/414344|jstor=414344|issn=0097-8507|url-access=subscription}}{{Cite journal|last=Troike|first=Rudolph C.|date=January 2015|title=Center-Embedding Relative Clauses in Coahuilteco|url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/679045|journal=International Journal of American Linguistics|volume=81|issue=1|pages=133–142|doi=10.1086/679045|s2cid=141664014|issn=0020-7071|url-access=subscription}} === Subject-Object concord === In each of these sentences, the object ''Dios'' 'God' is the same, but the subject is different, and as a result different suffixes (''-n'' for first person, ''-m'' for second person, and ''-t'' for third person) must be present after the demonstrative ''tupo·'' (Troike 1981:663). {{interlinear|indent=3 |Dios tupo·-n naxo-xt'e·wal wako· |God DEM-{{gcl|1CON|First-person conjunct}} 1pS-annoy CAUS |'We annoyed God'}} {{interlinear|indent=3 |Dios tupo·-m xa-ka·wa xo e? |God DEM-{{gcl|2CON|Second-person conjunct}} 2S-love AUX Q |'Do you love God?'}} {{interlinear|indent=3 |Dios tupo·-t a-pa-k'tace·y |God DEM-{{gcl|3CON|third-person conjunct}} 3S-{{gcl|SUB|subordinate}}-pray(PL) |'that (all) pray to God'}} === Center-embedding Relative Clauses === Troike (2015:135) notes that relative clauses in Coahuilteco can appear between the noun and its demonstrative (NP → N (Srel) Dem), leading to a center-embedding structure quite distinct from the right-branching or left-branching structures more commonly seen in the world's languages. One example of such a center-embedded relative clause is the following: {{interlinear|indent=3 |saxpame· pinapsa·i [xami·n ei-Obj xa-p-xo·] tupa·-n |sins you (OBJ) {} 2-{{gcl|sub|subordinate}}-know DEM-{{gcl|1C|first-person conjunct}} |‘the sins '''(which) you know'''’}} The Coahuilteco text studied by Troike also has examples of two levels of embedding of relative clauses, as in the following example (Troike 2015:138): {{interlinear|indent=3 |pi·lam apšap’a·kani [ei-SUBJ pi·nwakta·j [Dios (∅) pil’ta·j a-pa-ta·nko] tuče·-t a-p-awa·y] tupa·-t |people good.PL {} things God (DEM) pronj 3-{{gcl|sub|subordinate}}-command DEM-{{gcl|3C|third-person conjunct}} 3-{{gcl|sub|subordinate}}-do.PL DEM-{{gcl|3C|third-person conjunct}} |‘(He will carry to heaven) the good people [who do the things [that God commands]]’.}} ==See also== *[[Coahuiltecan languages]] *[[Coahuiltecan people]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Bibliography== * Goddard, Ives (Ed.).
